blocks.text: Paphian birds, that is, doves. Indeed, like the karia of the Arabs, the scolopax too, or woodcock (rusticula), is a harbinger of rain. Gesner in Birds, p. 504: Some take the call of the lesser woodcock (the French call it beccassine), when heard, as a prognostic of rain. He goes on to say that the sound of its call is like that of a knife drawn across a saw. This seems to be what the Arabs mean when they attribute to the karia ترجيع [tarjīʿ], that is, a reciprocating call. So far, then, everything is quite similar. Yet the colour is different: in the karia it is green, at least on the back, while in the woodcock it is so mottled that it is very far from green. Moreover, although both birds are edible, David does not seem to hold the קורא kore in high esteem, and the Arabs celebrate the karia for no other reason than that it is among the prognostics of rain. Our woodcock, by contrast, is most renowned among the delicacies of the table and yields little to the partridge. Hence Martial, book 13, Epigram 76, under the heading Rusticula: [II, 636] Whether I am a woodcock or a partridge, what does it matter, if the taste is the same? The partridge is dearer; that is why it tastes better.

Finally, no one has written of the woodcock what Jeremiah wrote of the קורא kore: the kore gathers (or broods) and does not bring forth. I conclude, therefore, that the kore is a bird peculiar to those regions, distinct from the woodcock and yet not differing much from it ^{(2)}. Now I must say how the ancient and modern interpreters explain this word.

Kore קרא is rendered by the Greeks νυκτικόραξ [nyktikorax], nycticorax, at 1 Sam. XXVI, 20., but they were undoubtedly misled by a faulty reading. They had read קדא for קרא, Daleth for Resh, letters that are very similar to each other. The word קדא fell out of use among the Hebrews, but from it the Chaldeans formed קדיא and the Syrians ܥܕܝܢ, with Koph and Ayin interchanged, as when they say ܥܛܪ, vapour, for קטר, and ܥܪܝܐ, cold, for [II, 637] קריא. That this conjecture is correct is clear from the fact that elsewhere νυκτικόραξ [nyktikorax] in the Greek version corresponds to the Hebrew כוס, for which the Chaldee Onkelos has קריא at Levit. XI, 17., and the Syriac translator ܒܣܢ at Psal. CII, 7. Therefore כוס and קרא, whence קריא and ܒܣܢ, are synonyms. Thus, if כוס is νυκτικόραξ [nyktikorax], as the Greeks render it, so too is קרא. A similar error occurs in the Talmudic tractate Niddah, fol. 23a, where instead of קריא with Daleth, קריא with Resh is written eight times, as if it were the bird kore, whereas it is a night bird. For קפופא kiphupha, that is, the owl, is joined with it. And they are said to be birds דעיניהן הולכות לפניהן כשלאדם, whose eyes are not at the side, as in other birds, but in the front, like those of humans. And in the Gloss both are described as עוף צועק בלילה ופניו דומות לחתול ועיניו לפניו, A bird that cries at night, with a face like a cat's and eyes in the front. Again in Berakhot, ch. 9, fol. 57b: כל מינין עופית יפין לחלום חוץ מן קריא וקפופא וקורפראי, All species of birds are auspicious in dreams, except the nycticorax, the owl and the bat. In these words too, I say, קריא is written with Resh, which must be changed to Daleth. So finally in the Chaldee [col. 84] paraphrase of Es. XXXIV, 15., for וקורידהון ינצפון בטולה read וקודידהון, And their nycticoraces will howl in its shade. For there too Resh stands for Daleth. This is why the Latin translator of the Chaldee rendered it thus: And the partridges will chatter, etc. This is utterly absurd. For the subject is the devastation of Idumaea, to which it is not fitting that partridges should chatter in it, but that nycticoraces and eagle-owls should howl in a dreadful manner.
